message.content:
I heard, then, that near Naucratis in Egypt there lived one of the ancient gods of that region, the one whose sacred bird is called the ibis; and the god’s own name was Theuth. It was he who first invented number and calculation, geometry and astronomy, as well as checkers and dice, and, above all, the written word. 

At that time Thamus was king over all Egypt, ruling from the great city of the upper country that the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, just as they call its god Ammon. Theuth went to him, displayed his arts, and declared that they ought to be shared with the rest of the Egyptians. The king asked what benefit each art possessed, and as Theuth explained, Thamus praised or criticized each one according to whether he thought it was well or poorly described. 

Thamus is said to have expressed many opinions to Theuth on both sides of every art, which would take too long to recount. But when they came to writing, Theuth said, "O King, this branch of learning will make the Egyptians wiser and improve their memory; for I have discovered an elixir of memory and wisdom."

Thamus replied, "O most ingenious Theuth, one person has the ability to give birth to the arts, but another must judge what share of harm or benefit they will bring to those who are to use them. And now you, as the father of writing, have out of affection attributed to it the exact opposite of its real power. For this invention will produce forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn it, because they will neglect their memory. Relying on writing, they will be reminded from the outside by alien marks, not from within by their own efforts. You have not discovered an elixir of memory, but of reminding. 

"And as for wisdom, you offer your pupils its appearance, not its reality. For having heard many things without instruction, they will imagine they know a great deal, though for the most part they will remain ignorant; and they will be difficult to associate with, having become wise in their own conceit rather than truly wise."
